title: Non-invasive assessment and quantification of liver steatosis by ultrasound, computed tomography and magnetic resonance.

Non-invasive assessment and quantiﬁcation of liver steatosis
by ultrasound, computed tomography and magnetic resonanceq
Nina F. Schwenzer1, Fabian Springer1, Christina Schraml1, Norbert Stefan2,
Jürgen Machann1, Fritz Schick1,*

2

Hepatic steatosis is the most prevalent liver disorder in the developed world. It is closely associated with features of metabolic syndrome, especially insulin resistance and obesity. The two most common conditions associated with fatty liver are
alcoholic liver disease (ALD) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Liver biopsy is considered the gold standard
for the assessment of liver fat, but there is a need for less invasive diagnostic techniques. New imaging modalities are emerging,
which could provide more detailed information about hepatic tissue or even replace biopsy. In the present review, available
imaging modalities (ultrasound, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging and proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy) are presented which are employed to detect or even quantify the fat content of the liver. The advantages and disadvantages of the above-mentioned imaging modalities are discussed. Although none of these techniques is able to diﬀerentiate
between microvesicular and macrovesicular steatosis and to reveal all features visible using histology, the proposed diagnostic
modalities oﬀer a wide range of additional information such as anatomical and morphological information non-invasively. In
particular, magnetic resonance imaging and proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy are able to quantify the hepatic fat content hence avoiding exposure to radiation. Except for proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy, all modalities oﬀer additional
information about regional fat distribution within the liver. MR elastography, which can estimate the amount of ﬁbrosis, also
appears promising in the diﬀerentiation between simple steatosis and steatohepatitis.

1. Introduction
Hepatic steatosis summarizes a wide spectrum of conditions characterized by triglyceride accumulation
within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes. The two most common conditions associated with fatty liver are alcoholic
liver disease (ALD) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
(NAFLD) which is related to obesity, insulin resistance
and metabolic syndrome. NAFLD is the most prevalent
chronic hepatic disease in the Western countries aﬀecting more than 30% of adults and 38% of obese children
[1,2]. In particular, males and certain ethnic groups, e.g.
Hispanics and Asian-Indians tend to have higher rates

of fatty liver. The term NAFLD describes a condition of
fat accumulation in the liver in the absence of excessive
alcohol consumption (less than 20 g per day) and speciﬁc causes of hepatic steatosis. Among them nutritional
(e.g. malnutrition and rapid weight loss), metabolic (e.g.
abetalipoproteinemia and lipodystrophy) and druginduced (e.g. glucocorticoids and methotrexate) causes
as well as other conditions (e.g. hepatitis C, jejunal diverticulitis with bacterial overgrowth, and inﬂammatory
bowel disease) are relevant [1].
Besides simple steatosis with histological signs of fat
accumulation in hepatocytes only, more severe states
exist: they are characterized by hepatic mononuclear cell
inﬁltration, hepatocyte necrosis and inﬂammation (nonalcoholic steatohepatitis or NASH) representing a major
risk factor for progression to liver failure, cirrhosis and
hepatocellular carcinoma [1,3,4]. In addition, NAFLD
is strongly associated with metabolic diseases like insulin
resistance and atherosclerosis, which is independent of
other risk factors as total and visceral adiposity [5–9].
Of particular interest, in obese subjects fatty liver
appears to be a stronger determinant of insulin resistance and earlier markers of atherosclerosis than total
and visceral adiposity [7]. Moreover, NAFLD is becoming increasingly recognized as a condition strongly and
directly involved in the pathogenesis of the epidemically
spreading metabolic diseases type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease [5]. As underlying hepatic molecular
mechanism fatty acids in the liver promote conditions
resulting in systemic subclinical inﬂammation, increased
hepatic glucose production, and, as recently described,
increased secretion of fetuin-A [5–9]. This protein qualiﬁes as a hepatokine because it is increasingly produced
and secreted from the liver under hepatic steatosis
[10,11] and directly induces insulin resistance [12] and
increased cytokine expression [13] in animals and
humans. Furthermore, serum levels of fetuin-A predict
incident diabetes, myocardial infarction and stroke in
large prospective studies [14–17]. Both, ALD and
NAFLD may lead to steatohepatitis with inﬂammation,
cell injury and ﬁbrosis and may progress to irreversible
cirrhosis [18–23].
Several approaches have been undertaken to prevent
and treat NAFLD. In particular moderate lifestyle intervention is considered the ﬁrst-line therapy [24,25]. However, response to the intervention varies among subjects
most probably due to genetic variation in candidate
genes for fatty liver and cardiorespiratory ﬁtness at
baseline [26–28]. Numerous clinical trials with pharmaceutical agents have also been undertaken in the recent
years; however, there is no ﬁnal consensus on the eﬀectiveness of such treatment [29,30].
Liver biopsy and histological analysis are considered
the diagnostic reference standard for the assessment of
fatty liver. Histological assessment provides information
about the fat distribution within the hepatic lobules and

allows for a semi-quantitative evaluation of steatosis
[31]. Microscopically, the steatosis pattern can be
divided into macro- and micro-vesicular steatosis with
hepatocytes containing either one large vacuole of fat
which is larger than the hepatocyte nucleus and displaces the nucleus or many small fatty cytoplasmatic
inclusions without a signiﬁcant nuclear displacement
[32].
Macro-vesicular steatosis is more common and is
found in NAFLD but also in alcoholic fatty liver disease [33]. In contrast, micro-vesicular steatosis is generally a more severe form of steatosis and is seen in a
variety of conditions such as toxicity of several medications, defect in beta-oxidation of fatty acids, Reye’s
syndrome but also in alcoholism. Although the pathogenesis is not clearly understood, an impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation seems to be an underlying
factor [34–36].
The extent of hepatic steatosis is visually estimated
based on the percentage of hepatocytes containing visible fatty inclusions, whereas the size of the intracellular
fat inclusions is not considered [37]. Diﬀerent scales representing the degree of steatosis are used ranging from
three- to six-point scales [32,37–41]. Often, a ﬁve-point
ordinal scale is used (0%, 1–5%, 6–33%, 34–66%,
P67%). Furthermore, it is possible to distinguish steatohepatitis from ‘‘simple steatosis” based on biopsy due to
assessment of extent of necroinﬂammatory activity,
ﬁbrosis and architectural alterations [42]. Standard liver
biopsy can be rapidly performed and is widely accepted.
Nevertheless, it is an invasive method with the risk of
post-interventional haemorrhage and bleeding although
the post-interventional complication rate seems to be
quite low [43,44]. The mortality rate lies between 0.1%
and 0.01% [44]. However, it must be taken into account
that biopsy-based quantiﬁcation of steatosis is derived
from a small tissue sample and may, therefore, be misleading in cases of uneven fat distribution in the liver.
Thus, non-invasive techniques are desirable to estimate
or even quantify the degree of steatosis and NASH
and eventually assess the pattern of hepatic fat
distribution.
The assessment of hepatic steatosis plays an important role in the preoperative evaluation of liver donors
for transplantation [45,46]. Especially the macro-vesicular subtype is critical for donor selection which has been
associated with a greater risk of primary nonfunction
after transplantation [47–49]. Another area of application is the monitoring of steatosis following treatment,
especially after dietary and lifestyle intervention since
repeated measurements are desirable [50,51].
This article will focus on diﬀerent imaging modalities
(ultrasound, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging) and discuss their practical applicability
for the diagnosis and quantitative assessment of liver
steatosis in clinical routine.

2. Ultrasound
In ultrasound (US) images, hepatic steatosis appears
as a diﬀuse increase in echogenicity due to the increased
parenchymal reﬂectivity caused by intracellular accumulation of fat inclusions (Fig. 1). Ultrasound is accepted
as an initial screening for fatty liver since it is non-invasive, inexpensive and widely available [52–55]. Nevertheless, the sensitivity and speciﬁcity of ultrasound in
detecting hepatic steatosis are a constant matter of
debate. The previous studies demonstrated that ultrasonography has a sensitivity of 60–94% and a speciﬁcity of
66–95% in detecting fatty liver [55–59]. In most studies,
liver biopsy was used as the gold standard. The speciﬁcity could be increased up to 100% if known liver disease,
drug use or alcohol consumption were ruled out [60].
Several studies demonstrated that ultrasound cannot
reliably distinguish between ﬁbrosis and steatosis
[61,62]. Others concluded that it is possible to diﬀerentiate between ﬁbrosis and hepatic steatosis, at least at
higher degrees of ﬁbrosis leading to an increase in coarse
echoes without posterior beam attenuation [52,55].
Although ultrasound has been shown to have an acceptable level of sensitivity it does not provide reproducible
quantitative information. Most ultrasound studies refer
to a three or more point scoring system for fatty liver
(‘mild’, ‘moderate’ and ‘severe’) [55,60] based on hyperechogenic liver tissue, the increased discrepancy of echo
amplitude between liver and kidney and the loss of echoes from the walls of the portal system.
One major weakness of ultrasound is its operator
dependency. In a retrospective ultrasound study, liver
steatosis was evaluated by three independent, experienced radiologists in 168 patients. The examination
was repeated one month later and the inter- and intraobserver variability was calculated. The mean interand intra-observer agreement rates for the presence of

435

increased liver fat were 72% and 76%. Intra-observer
agreement for severity of fatty liver ranged from 55%
to 68% [63]. These results reﬂect the high dependency
on subjective impression by the examiner. These ﬁndings
are in accordance with the results from Fishbein et al.
[39] which correlated needle biopsy, MRI measurements
and ultrasound ﬁndings in a fatty liver. They concluded
that ultrasound may be unreliable in the discrimination
of slight alterations in hepatic fat content.
Overall, ultrasound is an established tool used as a
screening modality with acceptable sensitivity and speciﬁcity in detecting fatty liver. Nevertheless, the drawbacks of this technique include its inaccuracy in
diﬀerentiating ﬁbrosis from steatosis, in reproducibility
and in exact quantiﬁcation of fat accumulation.

3. Computed tomography
Since the introduction of computed tomography (CT)
in the 1970s, the use of CT in diagnosis of hepatic steatosis has been evaluated by various investigators [64–
66]. CT provides an accurate and a reliable visualization
of the whole liver, so that not only diﬀuse but also focal
fatty inﬁltrations of the liver parenchyma can be accurately diagnosed. Hepatic steatosis is best visible in
non-enhanced CT images and presents with decreased
attenuation values of the parenchyma (i.e. hypodense
liver) due to the inverse relationship between hepatic
fat content and hepatic attenuation [54,67,68] (Fig. 2).
For assessment of hepatic steatosis mainly three measures were investigated including the absolute measurement of attenuation values which are given in
Hounsﬁeld units (HUs), the diﬀerence in attenuation
values between liver and spleen as well as the calculation
of the spleen-to-liver attenuation ratio. Normal, healthy
liver has an attenuation value of about 50–57 HU which

is about 8–10 HU higher than the one of spleen [69].
Attenuation values of the liver which are less than 40
HU or 10 HU smaller than those of the spleen are highly
predictive of hepatic steatosis [70,71]. In this case, the
liver parenchyma appears darker than the spleen and
even darker than the content of the hepatic vessels.
In contrast to the absolute attenuation values others
proposed spleen-to-liver attenuation ratios greater than
1.1 to be suggestive of at least a moderate hepatic steatosis
[72]. The spleen was introduced as an internal control in
order to reduce errors in CT attenuation caused by variations in CT parameters due to individual factors (such as
body size, body shape and metallic instruments). Being
aware of the limitations of pure measurement of attenuation values the usefulness of reference test objects containing various concentrations of fatty ﬂuids was tested.
Applying this technique, Ricci et al. demonstrated that
CT attenuation values can be accurately correlated to a
certain degree of hepatic steatosis [53]. Park and colleagues investigated absolute and relative CT attenuation-based methods of quantifying the degree of hepatic
steatosis in transplant donors. They found that diagnostic
performance of non-enhanced CT provides high performance in qualitative diagnosis of higher (>30%) degrees
of hepatic steatosis [71] with 100% speciﬁcity and 82% sensitivity using histologic analysis as the reference standard.
In order to reduce radiation exposure non-enhanced
CT images of the liver are not usually obtained for every
patient. Thus, the use of contrast-enhanced CT images
for the assessment of hepatic steatosis has been evaluated [73–75]. It was shown that various parameters such
as injection rate of intravenous contrast agents and timing of the measurement signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the attenuation values for liver and spleen and subsequently the
thresholds for determining hepatic steatosis. These limitations were further addressed in a study by Panicek and
co-workers [76] who demonstrated that, in contrastenhanced CT images, assessment of fatty liver is more
speciﬁc using skeletal muscle as standard reference.
However, the proposed comparison works only if the
degree of fatty inﬁltration is severe.

It should be considered, that underlying diﬀuse liver
diseases may alter attenuation values of liver parenchyma so that hepatic steatosis may be misdiagnosed.
Moreover, increased iron deposition in liver parenchyma in case of hemochromatosis may lead to a significant increase in attenuation values of the liver (see
Fig. 2C). Subsequently, the increase of attenuation due
to iron deposition and the decrease due to fatty inﬁltration might add up to almost normal attenuation values,
so that hepatic steatosis can be masked [77,78].
With the recent introduction of dual-source/dualenergy CT scanners the possibility of acquiring CT
images with diﬀerent energy levels in the same breath
hold might relativize results of former studies of the liver
[79,80]. First studies indicate, that dual techniques can
be used for measuring the extent and grade of fatty liver
[80]. The value of dual-energy CT in the clinical assessment of steatosis, however, has to be evaluated in further studies.
Although attenuation values of liver parenchyma
have been proven to correlate with hepatic steatosis on
non-contrast-enhanced CT images one has to be aware
that especially for small fractions of fatty inﬁltration this
is not an accurate and reliable marker [71]. Furthermore, it has recently been demonstrated in vitro that
CT attenuation values vary signiﬁcantly between diﬀerent manufactures’ multi-detector row CT (MDCT) scanners, among diﬀerent generations of MDCT scanners
and even with individual combinations of scanner and
convolution kernel [81]. Moreover, CT is associated
with radiation exposure which limits its use in longitudinal studies and in children. This leads us to the conclusion that for diagnosis of mild to moderate hepatic
steatosis CT is not clinically acceptable.

4. Magnetic resonance
The physical basis for determination of fat content in
a speciﬁed tissue by methods of magnetic resonance
(MR) is the so-called chemical shift. This means that


N.F. Schwenzer et al. / Journal of Hepatology 51 (2009) 433–445

the resonance frequencies of hydrogen nuclei depend
slightly on the chemical bond. The diﬀerence of resonance frequencies between hydrogen protons bound to
methylene groups of triglycerides (CH2 in fatty acid
chains) and water (H2O) protons amounts to approximately 220 Hz at 1.5 Tesla (T) magnetic ﬁeld strength
(or 3.3 parts per million (ppm)). This diﬀerence is very
small in comparison to the absolute resonance frequency
of approximately 64 MHz and is given usually in dimensionless units (ppm). The chemical shift eﬀect is directly
visible in MR spectra, displaying signals in dependence
on their resonance frequency. On the other hand the
chemical shift eﬀect can be used in diﬀerent ways in
order to generate MR images with information on fat
content. Several clinically feasible techniques are
described in the following sections.
4.1. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H MRS)
1

H MRS allows non-invasive studies in the molecular composition of tissues in vivo. Signals from metab-

437

olites with at least millimolar concentrations can be
detected from the selected volumes of interest with a
size of several ccm. 1H spectra from liver tissue
recorded in vivo usually show only two dominant signal
portions, namely the water signal (positioned at
4.7 ppm) and the signal from methylene protons of
fatty acids (positioned at 1.3 ppm) (Figs. 3 and 4). It
should be mentioned that some liver tumors might
show an additional signal from choline which can be
observed at 3.3 ppm [82,83].
MRS of the liver has been performed for many years,
beginning in 1993, where Longo et al. showed for the
ﬁrst time an excellent agreement between MRS and histomorphometry and data from CT [84,85]. Correspondence to bioptic results has been established in further
studies [50,86,87]. Several strategies are applied for volume-selective 1H MRS in vivo: single-voxel spectroscopy
(SVS) techniques, PRESS (point resolved spectroscopy)
[88] or STEAM (stimulated-echo acquisition mode)
sequences [89] are usually applied for recording spectra

to 27 ccm (3  3  3 ccm). Suitable voxels for spectroscopy can be easily positioned in a subregion of the liver
without inclusion of subcutaneous or visceral adipose
tissue – and remote to lung tissue. More detailed information is obtainable by MR spectroscopic imaging,
generating 2-dimensional or even 3-dimensional matrices of spectra [90,91]. However, due to the longer acquisition time (at least 10 min in comparison to about
2 min for SVS) this technique is rarely used for liver
examinations [92,93]. In most cases of NAFLD, hepatic
lipids seem to be distributed relatively homogeneously
in the liver [94–96] and therefore, SVS approaches
are considered representative for a reliable quantiﬁcation of hepatic lipids. However, it should be mentioned
that Cowin et al. showed signiﬁcant diﬀerences between
diﬀerent regions in right and left lobe in his study
[50].
Besides liver biopsy, which is the current standard of
reference for the diagnosis and grading of hepatic steatosis, 1H MRS of the liver has emerged to be a fast, safe,
non-invasive alternative for the quantiﬁcation of hepatic

fat content. Good reproducibility of liver MRS has been
determined, revealing high intra-individual correspondence in repeated measurements, e.g. in [50,95,97]. It is
important to note in this context that percentage values
of liver steatosis from MR spectroscopy studies (and
from MR imaging studies as well) are clearly diﬀerent
from percentage values from histological examinations.
The reason is that MR techniques determine volume
fractions of lipids in the liver tissue rather than the percentage of hepatocytes showing visible fat droplets in
the microscopic view. Besides the traditional interpretation by a pathologist an automated software for analysis
of photomicrographs has also been proposed by Marsman et al. [98]. Thus, the determination of liver fat content in biopsies could be simpliﬁed. On the other hand,
the results gained with the automated software and by
the visual estimation of the pathologist cannot be compared: the automated software measures the speciﬁc surface area of fat droplets in the microscopic ﬁeld, whereas
the pathologist estimates the overall area involved by
steatosis.

It should be mentioned that 1H MRS is not available
on all clinical scanners and remained a research tool up
to now, despite the fact that almost all commercially
available MR scanners operating at a ﬁeld strength of
1.5 T or higher have MRS capabilities (adequate Software must be installed by the manufacturer including
spectroscopy sequences, and additional post-processing
tools for the evaluation of the spectra are mandatory).
1
H MRS is being used in a large population studies to
determine the prevalence of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in the general adult population [97] and also in an
increasing number of longitudinal clinical studies [99–
104]. In cross-sectional studies it has also been shown,
that hepatic lipids strongly depend on hormonal and
genetic background of the subjects [26,105–114].
Apart from MR spectroscopy, chemical shift-based
MR imaging techniques, which enable to distinguish signal portions from water and fat in combination with
spatial information, are useful for the detection of hepatic steatosis in clinical practice. Diﬀerent imaging strategies with their inherent advantages and drawbacks are
described in the following sections.
4.2. Fat-sensitive MR imaging techniques based on signal
phase
The so-called in-opposed-phase MRI techniques use
the frequency diﬀerence between water and lipid signals
for generation of in-phase (IN) and opposed-phase (OP)
images. Depending on the chosen echo time TE the signal intensity of the water and fat net magnetization vectors are at a maximum (IN, 0° phase diﬀerence between
water and fat, in-phase conditions) or at a minimum
(OP, 180° phase diﬀerence between water and fat,
opposed-phase conditions) (Figs. 3 and 4). As mentioned, at 1.5 T, the resonance frequencies of fat and
water are separated by approximately 220 Hz, resulting
in a 180° phase shift between fat and water at intervals
of 2.32 ms [115–117]. The hepatic fat content can be
quantiﬁed by measuring the degree of signal intensity
loss on the OP images relative to the IN images
[118,119].
While conventional spin-echo sequences have acquisition times of several minutes for the whole liver, the
development of fast gradient echo techniques and parallel imaging [120,121] has reduced acquisition time suﬃciently to permit breath-holding techniques and, since
the IP and OP images are acquired simultaneously, misregistration errors are reduced [122]. Those fast gradient
echo techniques are now usually applied in clinical practice [119,123–125].
In the original two-point Dixon method for water
and fat-selective MR imaging, a slight timing oﬀset of
the 180° refocusing pulse was used in a spin-echo
sequence to create an OP condition without altering
echo time [115]. Since then, many modiﬁcations of the

439

Dixon method have been reported [116,122,126,127].
One has to consider that IN and OP images usually
are provided in magnitude format, wherein all phase
information is lost, but it eﬃciently reduces other
adverse eﬀects, such as those caused by inhomogeneity
in the magnetic ﬁeld. Without phase information, however, one cannot distinguish which constituent (water or
fat) is dominant in a given picture element. This can
pose a problem for hepatic tissue since a variety of metabolic and toxic conditions can lead to fat fractions of
more than 50% in the liver. To overcome this ambiguity,
a phase-sensitive processing has been proposed. This
method (three-point Dixon method) requires the acquisition of an additional image with a phase shift of 180°
or 360° and elaborated phase-correction algorithms to
obtain true fat-only and true water-only images [128–
136]. Unfortunately, the necessity of recording several
images for the Dixon method from the liver is critical,
due to the restricted duration of a breath-hold of the
patient. On the other hand, several measurements in different breath-hold periods suﬀer from potentially variable positions of the liver in the ﬁxed coordinate
system of the scanner.
One general limitation of the in-opposed-phase techniques is, that in the resultant fat-only and water-only
images, relaxation eﬀects cannot be completely ruled
out (T1 and T2*) [73,76,137] so that hepatic fat content
may be misdiagnosed. The relaxation times can be measured separately and considered in the fat calculation
but additional measurement of relaxation times leads
to increased examination times [122,138]. Nevertheless,
especially T2* eﬀects can cause severe problems in
patients with hepatic iron overload from either genetic
hemochromatosis or acquired iron overload. A high
concentration of iron within the hepatocytes can cause
relevant localized magnetic ﬁeld inhomogeneities, resulting in a signal loss of the liver parenchyma [32,123,125].
Insuﬃcient signal yield, however, may render accurate
fat quantiﬁcation impossible. Therefore, Alustiza and
Castiella proposed to perform a study of iron quantiﬁcation in cases of markedly decreased signal intensity inphase images [123].
Reeder et al. have developed the so-called IDEAL
technique [139], combining iterative decomposition of
water and fat with echo asymmetry and least-squares
estimation. This technique describes a multipoint fat–
water separation using optimized echo shifts in order
to achieve maximal SNR (signal-to-noise) performance.
Combined with gradient echo imaging it provides robust
fat–water separation even in the presence of inhomogeneities of the static magnetic ﬁeld [140]. In a next step,
Liu et al. proposed a reduction of the eﬀects of T1 bias
and noise bias by small- or dual-ﬂip angle approaches
(T1 bias), and magnitude discrimination and phaseconstrained methods (noise bias), which might inﬂuence
the correct determination of hepatic fat content [141].

However, this is still an experimental approach and clinical validation remains to be done.
4.3. Fat-selective MR imaging based on frequency
selective excitation
Selective imaging and quantiﬁcation of fat content
in the liver can be obtained by techniques operating
with so-called spectral–spatial excitation [142]. This
approach combines chemical shift selectivity with
simultaneous slice-selective excitation in gradient-echo
or spin-echo imaging sequences. Chemical shift selectivity is given by a series of six equidistant excitation
pulses (time period between pulses: 2.38 ms), resulting
in the excitation of a frequency band covering the
chemical shift range of methylene and methyl signals
of fatty acids (0.8–2.0 ppm) and leaving the potential
water signal contribution under the noise level.
Results gained from former investigations, which compared the spectral–spatial imaging with 1H MRS are
promising: the technique provides a high sensitivity,
especially for the assessment of small amounts of fat
with additional spatial information [95,117,142]. Nevertheless, a homogeneous static magnetic ﬁeld over
the recorded slice is required, which makes appropriate preparation (the so-called shimming) mandatory.
In contrast to the IN/OP method, the fat-selective
spectral–spatial gradient-echo sequence oﬀers less soft
tissue contrast, since only fatty components are visualized (Figs. 3 and 4). On the other hand, it allows for
fat quantiﬁcation without the necessity of T1 or T2*
corrections [143] and directly depicts fatty liver without the need to evaluate two or more images in order
to obtain the desired information. As an internal reference for pure fat with a volume fraction of lipids
close to 100%, nearby subcutaneous or visceral adipose tissue can be chosen. Not all but an increasing
number of commercial scanners oﬀer suitable
sequences with ‘‘fat selective excitation”. Comparable
to fat quantiﬁcation by MR spectroscopy the abovementioned techniques provide the volume fraction of
fatty tissue in the liver.
Apart from fat imaging, MR techniques additionally
allow for non-invasive assessment of other tissue characteristics of the liver during the same examination:
hepatic iron can be assessed using T2 and T2* measurements. O’Reagan et al. presented a method that
overcomes the need for additional T2* correction in
dual-echo methods. He used a breath-hold spoiled
gradient-echo sequence with a seven-echo readout,
which allows for simultaneous quantiﬁcation of fat
content and T2* [144].
Another increasingly applied MR method of tissue
characterisation is diﬀusion weighted imaging which
reﬂects the molecular diﬀusion of water (Brownian
motion) in the examined tissue [145,146]. Liver ﬁbrosis

can be measured by MR elastography which is a noninvasive method based on viscoelastic properties of the
tissue [147]. Diﬀerentiation between hepatic steatosis
and steatohepatitis poses an important clinical problem.
Nevertheless, the exact diagnosis is important since
NASH is histologically progressive and can lead to cirrhosis whereas simple steatosis has a relatively benign
course although it is not totally without histological
consequences [148]. It has been shown that elastography
could be a useful tool in the staging of ﬁbrosis in NASH
[149]. Moreover, several studies indicate that elastography could be able to detect early stages of steatohepatitis
since not only ﬁbrosis but also other factors such as
inﬂammation and hepatic stellate cell activation and
transdiﬀerentiation might increase liver stiﬀness [150–
152]. As it was shown for the assessment of steatosis
the non-invasive staging of liver ﬁbrosis is a further challenge in current liver research [153].

5. Suitable MR scanners
Most clinical MR units work at a magnetic ﬁeld
strength of 1.5 T. In the past 5 years, there was a trend
towards higher ﬁeld strength even of clinical MR units
and a considerable number of 3.0 T systems had been
already installed. Spectral dispersion (due to the mentioned chemical shift eﬀect) increases linearly with the
magnetic ﬁeld strength, enabling a better separation of
the signals and higher signal yield at higher ﬁeld. However, in the liver, which is characterized by the two wellseparated signals of water and fat, higher ﬁeld strength
is not really advantageous or promising. Even the potentially higher signal yield is often compromised due to
uneven radiofrequency excitation in the abdomen. Nevertheless, lipid quantiﬁcation is still possible on 3.0 T
systems. It should be mentioned that (mainly older) systems operating at low magnetic ﬁeld strength (0.2–0.5 T)
and low-cost MR systems with an open magnet design
are still working in some hospitals. Unfortunately, most
of these systems are not capable of 1H spectroscopy or
fat-selective imaging. In addition, MR examinations
are relatively costly and are not suitable for patients
with claustrophobia, implanted electronic devices or certain metal implants.

6. Conclusion
In conclusion, several methods for non-invasive estimation of liver fat with inherent advantages and disadvantages exist. Liver biopsy is still considered as the gold
standard in the assessment of fatty inﬁltration, because
it is able to diﬀerentiate between simple steatosis and steatohepatitis based on histological evaluation of the tissue. Nevertheless, it is an invasive and a potentially

risky method for the patient with subjective estimation
of the fat content in a small tissue sample, which is
not necessarily representative for the whole organ.
Ultrasound is widely available, non-invasive and cost
eﬃcient but operator dependent and insensitive for
small amounts of fat. CT oﬀers a semi-quantitative
method for the assessment of hepatic steatosis but is
inﬂuenced by iron overload and comes with radiation
exposure. Magnetic resonance oﬀers imaging and spectroscopic methods for quantiﬁcation of fat with relatively high accuracy without any invasive procedures
or radiation exposure. It seems that magnetic resonance
techniques are especially helpful in many clinical cases,
where mainly quantitative data of lipid content in liver
are of interest. Follow-up studies for monitoring eﬀects
of therapeutic interventions on liver fat have become
much easier applying magnetic resonance-based
techniques.

第2页：继续介绍NAFLD、代谢综合征、肝活检局限和无创影像定量的临床需求。
第3页：介绍超声下肝脂肪变的回声特征、诊断效能和局限；Figure 1比较正常肝与脂肪肝超声图像。
第4页：介绍CT衰减值、肝脾比较、铁沉积和增强扫描影响；Figure 2展示正常肝、脂肪肝及血色病CT表现。
第5页：进入磁共振部分，说明脂肪与水质子的化学位移和1H-MRS定量原理；Figure 3展示正常肝影像与波谱。
第6页：讨论波谱体素放置、校准及准确性；Figure 4展示明显肝脂肪变的脂肪选择成像和高脂肪波谱。
第7页：说明1H-MRS的设备与标准化限制，并介绍基于同相/反相水脂信号的MRI定量方法及误差来源。
第8页：介绍频率选择性脂肪成像、扩散与弹性成像等技术，随后给出各方法比较和结论。
第9页：完成结论，强调超声、CT和MR各自适用场景及MRI/MRS定量优势，随后进入参考文献。
第10页：参考文献，涵盖脂肪肝病理、超声和CT诊断研究。
第11页：继续参考文献，重点涉及CT定量和磁共振水脂成像方法。
第12页：继续参考文献，涉及异位脂肪、MRS、MRI和肝纤维化评估。
第13页：结束参考文献，包含扩散成像和MR弹性成像研究。
